Book of Common Prayer
book uhv KOM-uhn PRAIR
noun (church history / liturgy)
From common (shared, public) + prayer; the English liturgy chiefly composed by Thomas Cranmer for the reformed Church of England.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Book of Common Prayer is the English-language liturgy of the reformed Church of England, chiefly the work of Archbishop Thomas Cranmer, first issued in 1549, revised in 1552, and settled in the form of 1662 that endured for centuries. It was a fruit of the English Reformation: where the medieval church had prayed in Latin that the people could not understand, Cranmer gave England public worship in her own tongue, with the Scriptures read in course, the Psalms appointed through the month, and the great prayers framed in a noble English that shaped the language itself. Its theology, in the reformed editions, set forth justification by faith, the sufficiency of Christ's one sacrifice, and a Lord's Supper that turned away from the Mass toward a spiritual feeding by faith — though it kept an episcopal frame and forms of churchmanship the Puritans judged still half-reformed, and over which much later contention arose. This dictionary, holding a Baptist confession and the regulative principle, does not adopt a set liturgy as binding; yet it honors the Book of Common Prayer as a monument of the English Reformation, a vehicle that carried Scripture and reformed doctrine into the worship and memory of a whole people, and a treasury of biblical English prayer.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The English liturgy of the reformed Church of England, chiefly Cranmer's work (1549, 1552, settled 1662) — public worship in the people's tongue, with Scripture read in course and reformed doctrine in noble English. Honored as a monument of the English Reformation, though not adopted as binding by this Baptist dictionary.

BOOK OF COMMON PRAYER, noun. The English liturgy of the reformed Church of England.

Chiefly composed by Archbishop Thomas Cranmer; first issued 1549, revised 1552, settled 1662.

Gave England public worship in her own tongue, with Scripture and the Psalms read in course.

Set forth justification by faith and turned from the Mass toward a spiritual feeding by faith.

Kept an episcopal frame the Puritans judged still half-reformed.

📖 Key Scripture

1 Cor 14:15 — "I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the understanding also: I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the understanding also."

Col 3:16 — "Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom."

John 4:24 — "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth."

1 Cor 14:40 — "Let all things be done decently and in order."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Book of Common Prayer is corrupted from two sides: by the Anglo-Catholic revival that read the reformed liturgy back toward the Mass and priestly sacrifice it was framed to leave behind, and by a modern revision that has often diluted its biblical doctrine into vague and inclusive sentiment.

expand to see more

The first corruption is the Anglo-Catholic and Tractarian effort to undo the Reformation within the Prayer Book — reading Cranmer's reformed communion service as a sacrifice of the Mass, restoring the altar and the priesthood it was written to reject. The dictionary reads the reformed editions as their authors meant them: a turning from the Mass toward worship in spirit and in truth (John 4:24), with one finished sacrifice and a spiritual feeding by faith.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition of the historic text, which is fixed, but modern revisions have frequently softened its doctrine, trimming sin and judgment and inclusiveness of language at the cost of truth. The principle to recover is worship that joins spirit and understanding (1 Cor 14:15), letting the word of Christ dwell richly (Col 3:16), done decently and in order (1 Cor 14:40). The Book of Common Prayer at its best served that end; this Baptist dictionary honors it as a monument while holding that Scripture, not a fixed liturgy, governs the church's worship.
